h1: Georgia HOA Special Assessment Challenge Demand Letter
metaTitle: Georgia HOA Special Assessment Challenge Demand Letter
metaDescription: Challenge an unfair HOA special assessment in Georgia. Generate a state-specific demand letter citing POA Act protections and force your HOA to comply.
statuteCitation: O.C.G.A. § 44-3-220 et seq. (Georgia Property Owners' Association Act)
deadline: 30 days to respond before further legal action
penalty: Recovery of improperly collected assessments, attorney's fees, and court costs under O.C.G.A. § 44-3-232
introParagraph: If your Georgia homeowners association has hit you with a special assessment that seems excessive, unauthorized, or improperly approved, you have rights under state law. Georgia's Property Owners' Association Act (POA Act) and your community's recorded covenants strictly govern when and how an HOA board can impose special assessments. Many Georgia boards skip required steps—like proper notice, member voting thresholds, or budget transparency—hoping homeowners won't push back. A well-drafted demand letter citing the specific statute and your declaration's provisions often resolves the dispute without litigation. This page explains Georgia's special assessment rules, the legal arguments that work, and how to use a demand letter to challenge an assessment, recover wrongful charges, and protect yourself from improper liens or foreclosure threats.
lawExplanation:
Special assessments—those imposed beyond the regular annual budget for capital improvements, emergencies, or shortfalls—typically require strict compliance with the declaration's procedures. Most Georgia declarations require: (1) advance written notice to all members; (2) a duly called meeting with a quorum; (3) approval by a specified percentage of owners (often two-thirds or majority of those voting); and (4) a stated, lawful purpose tied to common expenses.

Georgia courts have consistently held HOAs to the plain language of their declarations, and ambiguities are typically construed against the association as drafter.
letterStrategy:
A demand letter is often the fastest, cheapest way to resolve a Georgia special assessment dispute. HOA boards and their management companies know that litigation is expensive and that courts in Georgia will scrutinize procedural compliance closely. A clear, well-cited letter signals you understand your rights and are prepared to escalate.

It's important to pay disputed amounts "under protest" in writing if you face foreclosure or lien risk while the dispute is pending—this preserves your right to recover funds without conceding the debt. Send the letter by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the HOA's registered agent (look it up on the Georgia Secretary of State's corporations database) and to the board president and management company. Keep copies of everything. If the HOA refuses to correct the issue, the letter becomes critical evidence of your good-faith effort and the board's bad faith—often supporting an attorney's fee award later.
proceduralNotes: Georgia magistrate (small claims) courts handle disputes up to $15,000 (increasing to $25,000 for actions filed on or after January 1, 2027) with no attorney required, making them a practical venue for refund claims. For claims over $15,000, or to seek injunctive relief like removing a lien or stopping foreclosure, you'll need to file in state or superior court. Georgia has a six-year statute of limitations on written contract claims (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-24), which generally covers declaration-based disputes. Consider consulting a Georgia HOA attorney before any sale date.

faq.q: Can my Georgia HOA impose a special assessment without a vote of the owners?
faq.a: It depends on your declaration. Most Georgia HOA declarations require owner approval—often a two-thirds vote at a properly noticed meeting—for special assessments above a certain amount or for non-emergency purposes. The board cannot override these requirements. If the board imposed the assessment unilaterally when a vote was required, the assessment is likely invalid and challengeable. Always read your recorded Declaration of Covenants and bylaws carefully to identify the exact procedure required for the type and amount of assessment in question.

faq.q: What is the Georgia Property Owners' Association Act and does it apply to my community?
faq.a: The POA Act, O.C.G.A. § 44-3-220 et seq., is Georgia's statute governing HOAs that have specifically opted in by recording submission language in their declaration. Not all Georgia HOAs are subject to it. Check your recorded declaration for language stating the community is submitted to the POA Act. If it applies, you gain additional statutory protections regarding assessments, liens, and governance. If not, your declaration, bylaws, and the Georgia Nonprofit Corporation Code govern instead.

faq.q: Can the HOA put a lien on my home or foreclose over a disputed special assessment?
faq.a: Yes, Georgia HOAs governed by the POA Act can record liens under O.C.G.A. § 44-3-232 and pursue foreclosure for unpaid assessments. However, the underlying assessment must be valid. If you successfully challenge the assessment as improperly imposed, the lien is unenforceable. Pay disputed amounts under written protest if foreclosure is threatened to preserve your refund rights, and consider seeking a court injunction. Act quickly—Georgia's nonjudicial foreclosure process moves fast once started.

faq.q: How long do I have to challenge an HOA special assessment in Georgia?
faq.a: Georgia's general statute of limitations for written contract claims, including HOA declaration disputes, is six years under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-24. However, you should challenge an improper assessment immediately—delay can be argued as waiver or acceptance, and unpaid amounts accrue interest, late fees, and lien risk. Send a demand letter as soon as you identify the defect, and pay any portion you don't dispute under written protest while the challenge is pending.

faq.q: Can I recover attorney's fees if I win my challenge against the HOA?
faq.a: Possibly. Many Georgia HOA declarations contain prevailing-party attorney's fee clauses that work both ways—if the HOA can collect fees from you, you can typically collect fees from the HOA when you win. Additionally, O.C.G.A. § 13-6-11 allows fee recovery where the defendant has acted in bad faith, been stubbornly litigious, or caused unnecessary trouble. Documenting the HOA's refusal to correct a clear violation after your demand letter strengthens any later fee request.
